pron_note: Also heard as dis-PA-ruht; the first-syllable stress is standard.
means:
Different in **kind**, not just in degree — so unlike that the things resist being compared or lumped together.

Two shirts of different colours are *different*; a shirt, a tax code and a whale are *disparate*. The word is usually doing one of two jobs: insisting that a comparison is illegitimate ("these are disparate cases"), or flagging that a collection is a grab-bag of mismatched parts ("**disparate** sources", "**disparate** systems"). Formal and analytical — it's the vocabulary of reports and arguments, not of conversation.
trap: ⚠️ **disparate ≠ desperate.** *Desperate* (DES-puh-ruht) is hopeless, frantic, willing to do anything. Nearly the same sound, opposite half of the dictionary — the GRE will happily exploit the eye-slip.
trick_line: **dis-PAR-ate = not on *par*.** Different things you can still rank; disparate things you can't even score on the same card.
trick_unpack: The hidden **par** ("equal") is the whole point: disparate items aren't merely unequal, they're not on comparable terms at all.
sentences: The committee's report stitched together **disparate** strands of evidence — census data, coroners' records, a century of parish registers — into a single argument.
Our team is five people from five **disparate** backgrounds, and somehow the standups still work.
in_the_wild: **"Disparate impact"** — the standard term in employment and housing law for a neutral-looking rule that lands unequally on different groups. If you've read a hiring-policy or compliance document, you've met the word there.
etymology: Sits in the family of Latin **par** = *"equal"* — the **par** of *parity*, *par for the course*, *peer*, and *disparity* (from **dispar**, "unequal"). Lock that root in and you get several GRE words at once.
one_line: So different in kind as to be incomparable.
